claim.why_it_matters: The heading levels invert the clause hierarchy. 16.2.1.2 is a fourth-level clause but is emitted at h2 - shallower than its own parent 16.2.1 (h3) and shallower than its sibling 16.2.1.1 (h4). Likewise 16.2.2 (third level) is at h2 while its peer 16.2.1 is at h3, and 16.2.2.1 / 16.2.2.2 sit at h3 while their peer 16.2.1.1 sits at h4. Any tool that builds an outline, a TOC, or a section-anchored citation index from the headings places 16.2.1.2 and 16.2.2 as top-level peers of the '## Page NNN' furniture rather than inside clause 16.2, so heading-tree citation lookup can fail to resolve 16.2.1.2 and 16.2.2.x.

verdict.reasoning: REFUTED on four independent grounds. (1) NOTHING IS MISSING. The kind label 'missing-heading' is a misnomer. I rendered spec_p972.png at 300 dpi and read it directly. The printed page carries exactly four headings - '16.2.1.2 General rules', '16.2.2 FactoryObject method', '16.2.2.1 General', '16.2.2.2 General rule' - and all four are present in specs/ISO_COBOL.md at lines 38833, 38840, 38843, 38848 with the clause number and the title text verbatim, including the plural/singular distinction the PDF actually prints ('General rules' for 16.2.1.2, which has two rules; 'General rule' for 16.2.2.2, which has one). The claim quotes both sources accurately; it simply does not identify any absent or altered content. (2) THE PDF ENCODES NO HEADING LEVEL TO LOSE. Looking at the printed glyphs myself: all four headings on p.972 are set in the SAME bold face at the SAME point size, with the same left margin and the same tab gap between number and title. The printed page distinguishes 16.2.2 (third-level) from 16.2.2.1 (fourth-level) by the clause NUMBER alone - there is no typographic level signal in the source. A markdown '#' count therefore transcribes nothing that exists in the PDF; it is a rendering choice made by the converter, so a 'wrong' count cannot be a PDF-vs-markdown content discrepancy. Per the rejection criteria this is formatting, and it changes no meaning. (3) THE PATTERN IS A DOCUMENT-WIDE CONVERSION CONVENTION, NOT A PAGE-972 DEFECT. The transcription is page-sliced, and each slice restarts its heading depth at h2 because the converter has no cross-page context. Measured over the whole file: of the 492 numbered headings that appear immediately after a '## Page NNN' marker, 473 (96%) are emitted shallower than their clause depth would imply - e.g. '## 4.2.5' (depth 3 at h2), '## 6.2.3.2 Syntax rules' (depth 4 at h2, exactly the same shape as 16.2.1.2), '## 5.2.3 Optional words'. Aggregate tallies show depth-4 clauses split 162/620/24 across h2/h3/h4 and depth-5 clauses split 118/128/41. Page 972 is one unremarkable instance of a global artifact. Filing it as a page-972 structural discrepancy in the reconciliation ledger would misattribute a whole-document formatting convention to this page. Note also that the relative nesting WITHIN the page slice is internally coherent (16.2.2 at h2 with 16.2.2.1/16.2.2.2 at h3 beneath it); only the absolute baseline resets at the page boundary. (4) THE STATED HARM DOES NOT OCCUR. The claim asserts that section-anchored citation lookup 'can fail to resolve 16.2.1.2 and 16.2.2.x'. It cannot: every one of these headings is immediately preceded by an explicit HTML anchor encoding the full clause path - line 38832 '', 38839 '', 38842 '', 38847 ''. Those anchors, plus the dotted clause number printed in the heading text itself, make the hierarchy fully machine-recoverable independent of the '#' count. Nothing in the citation path depends on heading depth. Body text was also checked word-for-word against the render and matches: both rules of 16.2.1.2 (including the '14.6.2.4, Initial state of object data' cross-reference and 'EC-OO-RESOURCE'), the 16.2.2.1 paragraph, rule 1) of 16.2.2.2, the NOTE, and both Invoke examples. The only textual difference anywhere on the page is that the PDF sets a double space in 'the methods of a factory object' where the markdown has a single space - pure whitespace, explicitly out of scope. No content discrepancy exists on page 972.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a PDF-vs-markdown discrepancy. All four headings are present with correct numbers and titles, and the page body matches the PDF word-for-word. The PDF sets every heading on this page in identical bold type and conveys hierarchy solely through the clause number, so no heading level was lost in transcription. The uneven '#' depths are a document-wide side effect of page-sliced conversion resetting heading depth at each page boundary - it affects 473 of the 492 numbered headings that follow a '## Page NNN' marker, so it is not a page-972 finding. If the project wants uniform heading depth it is a single global normalization pass (derive level from the dotted clause number), tracked as a transcription-quality task, not as a reconciliation ledger entry. The claimed citation-lookup failure does not occur: explicit '<a id="section-16-2-1-2">' / 'section-16-2-2' / 'section-16-2-2-1' / 'section-16-2-2-2' anchors precede each heading and encode the full clause path.
